# What the Graph Could Answer

> An analysis, not a proposal. Written 2026-08-06 against the schema as built, to answer two questions the operator asked: **what is missing from the basic graph relationships**, and **what is this graph actually good for**.
> 
> Parent: **The Library Graph** (Epic, P0). Nothing here overrides a decision that Epic took; where it revisits one, it says so.
## The graph as built
Fourteen tables. Six of them are edges.
| Edge | Connects | Rows (drive library) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `video_performer` | video → performer | 1,821 |
| `video_studio` | video → studio | 1,641 |
| `video_tag` | video → tag | 1,443 |
| `performer_tag` | performer → tag | 359 |
| `studio_parent` | studio → studio | 0 |
| `pending_tag_association` | staging | 0 |
The operator's summary was *"actors have tags and photos, videos have a file and tags, studios have parents and imprints."* That description omits the two busiest edges in the library: **videos have performers**, and **videos have a studio**. Those two are most of the graph.
**There are four node kinds, not three.** Tags are not `EntityProfile` rows — correction C1 in the Epic — but they have their own table, stable folded identity, a display name and a kind, and they attach to **two** different node kinds. That is a node by any working definition. Treating tags as an attribute is what produced the case-collision defect C6 describes.
## Part 1 — What is missing
### The structural gap: edges are bare pairs
Every edge table is `(from, to)` and nothing else. That single fact causes most of what follows.
An edge cannot currently carry:
- **A credited name.** The source supplies the name a performer appeared under in a specific scene, which often differs from their canonical one. It is a property of the *appearance*, not of the person or the video, so there is nowhere to put it and it is discarded.
- **Billing or role.** Which performer is the lead is an edge property.
- **Provenance.** D7 says every value carries its source. Edges do not — an edge asserted by a match and an edge inferred from a filename are indistinguishable after the fact.
- **Time.** See below; this is the big one.
### ⚠️ Two edges have no access to time at all
Every edge that touches a **video** inherits that video's `releaseDate` for free. That covers `video_performer`, `video_studio` and `video_tag` — three quarters of the graph is implicitly dated already.
`performer_tag` and `studio_parent` touch no video, so they are asserted as **eternal truths**, and neither is:
- A performer's hair colour, body attributes and even name change over a career. `performer_tag` says "this is true", not "this was true from 2016".
- An imprint is founded, acquired, absorbed and retired. `studio_parent` says a network owns an imprint with no sense of *since when* — so a video released before the acquisition is filed under a parent that did not own it at the time.
This is worth stating plainly because it caps what the temporal analysis in Part 2 can do. Everything routed through a video is answerable today; everything else needs an edge that can hold a date.
### Missing nodes and edges
| Gap | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Series** | Deliberate | `Asset.videoName` is free text. The Epic decided this explicitly — 5% of the library carries one. The obvious fifth node when that changes. |
| **video ↔ video, "same work"** | Not built | `VideoDuplicateAnalyzer` finds these and the verdict is never persisted, so it is rediscovered every run and the operator re-answers the same question. |
| **playlist → video** | Outside the graph | `playlists` / `playlist_items` are their own tables with a `position` column. Ordered membership — which a bare-pair edge table cannot express. |
| **node → external identity** | Stored as a column | D4 says *"a match is an edge to an external identity, and must be as durable as any other"*. It is `enrichmentSourceId`, a column. As an edge it would support several sources per node and a match history. |
| **performer ↔ performer** | Not built | AKAs are an array field. "These two records are one person" is not expressible, so a merge is destructive rather than an assertion. |
| **tag → tag (parent)** | Not built | Studios got a hierarchy; tags did not, though the shape is identical and more common — a broad tag properly contains several narrow ones. |
| **scene marker → tag** | Not built | `scene_markers` exist. A tag that applies to *part* of a video is a different and finer claim than one that applies to the whole. |
## Part 2 — What the graph could answer
Grouped by what they need, cheapest first. ⭐ marks the ones that need no schema change at all.
### A. Time, through the video node — buildable today
The pieces already exist and are not connected: `Asset.releaseDate`, `EntityProfile.birthDate` / `birthYear` / `careerStartYear` / `careerEndYear`, and **`AgeAtRelease`**, which already computes age at publication and — unusually carefully — distinguishes an **exact** answer from an **approximate** one, rendering the latter as a range so it can never be read as precise.
⚠️ `AgeAtRelease` is currently **display-only**. It appears in the inspector and the grid and nothing filters, sorts or groups by it. `ActorFilterCriteria` can ask *"who is 25 now"*; nothing can ask *"which videos did this person make at 25"*. That is the single largest gap between what the data supports and what the app offers.
⭐ **A career arc on the actor's profile page.** Group that performer's videos by their age at release, or by year, instead of one flat grid — the same sectioned treatment the studio family view just got. A performer's filmography read in order is a different object from a bag of videos.
⭐ **Age-at-release as a filter and a smart collection.** Everything needed exists; the honest form must filter on `possibleAges`, not `years`, or an approximate 18 silently includes 17.
⭐ **Recorded career span versus the evidence.** The source states `careerStartYear`; the library holds videos with dates. Where they disagree the answer is interesting either way — a video before the recorded start means the span is wrong or the match is.
### B. Studios in time — the operator's question
*"Studios feature different actors at different times — beginning of career, end of a career."* This is computable now: for each `video_studio` edge, take the video's release date and the performer's career start, and the difference is **career stage at time of release**.
⭐ **A studio's signature.** Aggregate that difference across a studio's catalogue and a studio acquires a character that is measured rather than asserted: one that consistently appears in the first two years of careers is a discovery house; one that appears in the last two is a late-career or redistribution label. This is the kind of claim no single record supports and the graph does easily.
⭐ **A studio's roster by era.** Which performers a studio worked with, bucketed by year — turnover, retention, and the point at which a roster changed over.
⭐ **Debuts.** The first video in the library for each performer, grouped by studio: which houses start careers.
**Imprint eras** (needs `studio_parent` populated, and ideally dated). The release-date range of each imprint's videos shows when it operated — a network's history as a timeline of labels launching and winding down. ⚠️ Without a date on `studio_parent` this describes when an imprint *released*, not when it was *owned*, and those differ across an acquisition.
### C. Tags in time — the operator's question
*"Actors' association with tags may intensify or wane."* `video_tag` × `video_performer` × release date gives this directly.
⭐ **Tag trajectory per performer.** The share of a performer's videos carrying a tag, by year. A tag in 10% of early work and 80% of recent is a trajectory, and a trajectory is a fact about a career that no individual video states.
⭐ **Vocabulary drift.** The same measure across the whole library says when a tag entered use and whether it is still in use — the library's own history, and a way to spot a tag that has been quietly superseded.
⭐ **Tag co-occurrence.** Tags that nearly always travel together are either duplicates awaiting a merge or a parent and child awaiting a hierarchy that does not exist yet. This is the evidence that would justify building tag parentage.
⭐ **Promotion evidence.** The Epic decided (C3, decision 2) that a performer-attribute tag sitting on a video is left alone for enrichment to correct, because *"an attribute read off a video is a guess about which of its cast it describes"*. That is right for one video. Across a performer's whole filmography it stops being a guess: a performer-attribute tag on 90% of the videos of a **single-performer** cast is strong evidence it belongs on the performer. The graph can now produce that evidence — to **offer**, never to apply.
### D. Genuinely graph-shaped questions
These need no new schema and are impossible without edges — they are the argument for the Epic.
⭐ **Two-hop discovery.** Performers who share a studio but have never shared a video. Reachable in one query, unanswerable from strings.
⭐ **Bridges.** Performers or studios whose removal would disconnect the graph — the records that link otherwise separate production circles. Ordinary centrality, and a genuinely different way to find something to watch.
⭐ **"More like this" by path, not by string.** Distance over shared performers, studio, family and tags, weighted. Tag-string similarity cannot see that two videos share a studio *family*; the graph can.
⭐ **Clusters.** Community detection over `video_performer` tends to recover real production circles without being told they exist.
### E. The graph auditing itself
The most valuable class, because these find **wrong data** rather than surface existing data.
⭐ **Age-at-release outliers.** A video whose date implies an implausible age for a credited performer is evidence of a bad match, a wrong birth date, or a wrong release date. A single record cannot be checked against itself; two joined records can.
⭐ **Career-span violations.** A performer credited on a video outside their recorded active years.
⭐ **Anachronistic studios.** A video released before the earliest evidence of its studio operating.
⭐ **Graph-shaped duplicate detection.** Same performers, same studio, same duration, different file — complements the perceptual hash, and catches the re-encodes and re-releases a hash misses.
⭐ **Roster implausibility.** A performer credited once at a studio, in a year they appear nowhere else, is worth a second look at the match.
### F. Needs new structure
| Idea | Needs |
| --- | --- |
| Credited-as names; billing order | Edge attributes |
| "This tag applies from 2016" | A date on `performer_tag` |
| Acquisition history | A date on `studio_parent` |
| Confirmed duplicates that stay confirmed | A `video_video` edge with a verdict |
| Tag hierarchy (broad ⊃ narrow) | A `tag_parent` edge — the same shape `studio_parent` already has |
| Several sources per node, match history | D4's match-as-edge |
## What this suggests doing first
Not a plan, but the ordering the analysis implies:
1. **Make ****`AgeAtRelease`**** a first-class dimension** — filter, sort, group. Everything needed exists, it is display-only today, and it unlocks most of section A and much of B.
2. **Career-arc sections on the actor profile**, reusing the sectioned-grid pattern now shared by the season view and the studio family view.
3. **The self-audit checks (E)** — cheap, and they find real errors rather than presenting existing data more attractively. A natural companion to Studio Health.
4. **Edge attributes** — the structural unlock. Worth designing before more edge kinds are added, because retrofitting a property onto six existing tables is harder than designing the seventh with one.

### Step 3, as built — "Impossible Data"
`GraphAudit` in `LibraryCore`, surfaced as **Settings → Find Problems → Impossible Data**. Four checks, all of which need two records joined and none of which any single record can answer:
| Check | Certain? |
| --- | --- |
| 🚨 Released before a credited actor was born | **Yes** |
| Implausible age at release (outside 15–85) | No |
| Released before the recorded career start | No |
| Released after the recorded career end | No |
⭐ **The first check found a real blind spot.** `AgeAtReleaseCalculator` guards `born <= released` and returns nil — correct for display, since it refuses to show a negative age — but it means the app renders this case as *"age unknown"* and **nothing anywhere said so**. The very care that keeps the age display honest is what hid the impossible records. A test pins that the calculator really is silent, so the audit is knowingly the only surface.
Design decisions worth keeping:
- ⚠️ **Only the first check is certain.** The others compare against a **recorded** career span, and spans from a source are frequently incomplete — an early credit is usually the record being wrong about the career rather than the video being wrong. The screen separates the two counts in its headline, because "9 findings" reads the same either way and they are not the same news.
- 🚨 **A missing ****`careerEndYear`**** means the span is OPEN**, not unknown — an existing decision in `EntityProfile`. Flagging recent work against it would have reported every active performer in the library.
- **An impossible date produces ONE finding, not four.** Every other check would be derived from the same impossible numbers and would only repeat it in other words.
- **Implausible ages are flagged only when EVERY possible age is outside the band**, the same conservatism as the age filter — an approximate age spans two values, and flagging a borderline one sends the operator to check a record that is fine.
- **It reports and does not repair, and unlike Studio Health it does not route either.** There is no fix tool because the audit cannot know which of the two records is wrong. Tapping a row opens the video and lets the operator decide.
- A finding names the **performer as well as the video**: the video is fine for everyone else in its cast.
**Not built from section E:** graph-shaped duplicate detection, which wanted same-cast + same-studio + same-duration. `Asset` carries no duration, so that check has no input without going through `VideoDuplicateAnalyzer`'s own machinery. Roster implausibility was left out as too noisy for a first pass.
## Evidence
Schema read at the current migration on 2026-08-06. Edge counts carried from the graph verification recorded in the previous session's handoff. `AgeAtRelease` usage established by reading its call sites: `InspectorView` and `AssetGridView`, both display; `AssetFilterCriteria` has no age field, and `ActorFilterCriteria`'s `minAge`/`maxAge` filter on a performer's age **today**, not at release.
## Step 4 completed 2026-08-07 — the credited name
⚠️ **Edge attributes were only half delivered.** Migration v29 added `credited_as` and `billing` to `video_performer` in the previous session, and **nothing ever wrote to them.** `VideoMetadataProposal.actors` was `[String]`, so the name a performer appeared under in a scene was read at the plugin boundary and dropped there. The column existed, the data existed, and the two were never connected. This analysis named it under section F — *"credited-as names; billing order → needs edge attributes"* — and the attributes shipped without it.
`actors` is now `[ProposedCredit]`: a canonical name, the name credited in this video, and a billing position where the source states one.
### 🚨 What finishing it uncovered — a performer-splitting bug
The plugin's `performerNames` **preferred the credited name** and used the canonical one only as a fallback. So a performer who worked under three aliases became **three separate profiles**, each holding part of a filmography, none holding all of it, and nothing recording that they were one person.
Nothing in 143 passing plugin tests pinned it either way, which is how it survived. The canonical name is now the identity; the credited name travels beside it as edge data.
⚠️ This is a **data-quality defect already in the library** — past matches filed performers under aliases. The split profiles are still there. Merging them is the actor-disambiguation tool's job, not a migration's, because only a person can say two profiles are one performer.
### Decisions worth keeping
- **The canonical name becomes the ****`actor:`**** tag, never the credited one.** Filing a performer under a name they used once is what created the splits.
- **Only credits that SAY something are stored.** A credit carrying neither a different name nor a billing position records that a performer was credited normally — which the edge already implies. Writing it for everyone would fill the column with rows that mean nothing and bury the few that matter. A credit differing only by case is the same name.
- ⭐ **Shown at review**, as *"Alice Smith (as Alicia S.)"*. A credited name that looks nothing like the performer is the clearest sign the source matched the wrong person, and hiding it discards the evidence at the one moment someone is looking.
- ⚠️ **The "Credited As" line on the inspector is deliberately not a browse pill.** Tapping it would search for a performer filed under a name the library does not use, and find nothing.
- **`ProposedCredit`**** is ****`ExpressibleByStringLiteral`**, so a plain name still reads as one and every fixture naming a performer and nothing else is unchanged.
**1,190 core tests + 153 plugin tests, 0 failures.** Both platforms build. D9 clean.
⭐ **Billing is carried but never inferred.** The source states it or it stays nil — the order a list happened to arrive in says nothing about billing, and deriving it would manufacture a fact.
